10351-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-v:
This tenth volume of Samuel Johnson's works, issued in 1825, holds another set of his parliamentary debates for the Gentleman's Magazine. Johnson recast second-hand reports into polished speeches, giving eighteenth-century politics a literary shape. A prefatory note defends open knowledge of national deliberations, against rulers who feared the press.

Debates treat corn export, seditious papers, the army, half-pay officers, Walpole's removal, Westminster cleansing, seamen, mutiny, and the queen of Hungary. Each debate shows speakers arguing law, war, and money with skill and passion. Readers get Johnson's powerful, if invented in form, version of Commons debate.
10352-the-works-of-samuel-johnson-ll-d-v:
This eleventh volume of Samuel Johnson's works, issued in 1825, holds his parliamentary debates, written for the Gentleman's Magazine. Johnson was not in the House; he recast reports of speeches into polished, readable prose, giving each speaker a clear voice. The volume thus reads as both history and literature, with Johnson's wit shaping every speech.

Debates cover addresses to the king, Hanoverian troops, the army, trade, navigation, and spirituous liquors. Lords and members from Argyle to Newcastle appear in the speaker lists, arguing law, war, and money with heat and humor. Readers get Johnson's vivid version of eighteenth-century politics, argument, and wit.
18675-modern-skepticism-a-journey-throug:
Joseph Barker published this life story at Philadelphia in 1874 with Smith, English and Company. A minister by trade, Barker traces his path from early faith and happy ministry through doubt and back again. Chapters name causes of unbelief: vice, dashed hopes about Christianity, mysteries of providence, human creeds that misstate Christ, church divisions, ignorant advocates, and false science.

Later chapters probe quarrels among ministers, his rationalizing bent, changes to his creed, and preachers who dress fancy as doctrine, with John Wesley as a test case. Barker writes frankly about his own mind and errors. The book is a candid Victorian record of faith lost and regained.
2708-colomba:
Prosper Merimee wrote this Corsican tale, translated by Lady Mary Loyd, opening in October 181- at Marseilles. Colonel Sir Thomas Nevil, an Irish officer of the English army, lands with his daughter after a tour in Italy, bound for an island ruled by vendetta.

Colomba, a fierce young Corsican woman, demands vengeance for her father's death, and draws the English visitors into a blood feud. Merimee writes with cool, exact prose, and his Corsica feels both beautiful and pitiless. The novella endures as a masterpiece of the vendetta tale, and of passion bound by honor.
29564-the-pearl-of-the-antilles-or-an-ar:
Walter Goodman, writing for Henry S. King and Company of London in 1873, called Cuba the pearl of the Antilles and told of it as an artist traveling there. The book is inscribed to his traveling companion and brother-artist, Senor Don Joaquin Cuadras of Cuba, in memory of long friendship at home and abroad. Goodman chose to treat his subject from an artist's point of view.

Cuba, he notes in his preface, had lately become a prominent object of attention for Europe and America. His pages mix travel, art, and social observation, with Spanish words kept in old spelling. Readers of Cuban history and travel writing will find a vivid, first-hand view of the island before its later wars.
31158-campaigning-in-cuba:
George Kennan's 1899 book, published by the Century Company, reports the Spanish-American War from the field. War broke out on April 21, 1898, and a week later the editors of the Outlook asked Kennan to sail with Clara Barton on the Red Cross steamer State of Texas. On May 5 he left Washington for Key West, then Tampa, where General Shafter's army of invasion was assembling.

Twenty-one chapters follow the Red Cross work, war correspondents and dispatch boats, Guantanamo, the landing, and Siboney. They go on to the battles of Caney and San Juan, the field hospital, the captured city of Santiago, Morro Castle, and fever in the army. Kennan's clear reporting makes the book a first-rate eyewitness history of the Santiago campaign.
33617-pioneering-in-cuba:
James M. Adams, one of the original colonists, narrates the settlement of La Gloria, the first American colony in Cuba, in this 1901 book. Adams lived in La Gloria for nearly half a year and served as chairman of the Pioneer Association's committee on the colony's history. He writes from first-hand knowledge of its early months. His preface promises a true story told without bias.

The narrative records daily happenings, incidents, and anecdotes of the pioneers: their arrival, their work, their cheerfulness under hardship, and the community they built. Adams dedicates the book to his fellow colonists, whose courage won his admiration. For readers interested in American expansion, tropical settlement, and frontier community life, it is a rare eyewitness record.
6020-cappy-ricks-retires-but-that-doesn-:
Peter B. Kyne brings back Cappy Ricks, retired but returning stronger than ever, in tales of the Blue Star Navigation Company. Readers meet Michael J. Murphy again, once chief kicker of the barkentine Retriever under Captain Matt Peasley, later her skipper with pleasure and profit to all concerned.

The illustrations promise a ship's log line about a lone survivor, a shout of two million dollars from J. Augustus Redell, and Cappy finding a girl a rich husband in time. Kyne writes brisk sea-business comedy, where old salts refuse to stay ashore. Retirement, in his world, is only a pause between ventures.
6392-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Nero ends the race of Caesars, an event foretold by signs, two of them striking, Suetonius says. When Livia, after marrying Augustus, visited her villa at Veii, an eagle dropped a hen into her lap. The hen held a laurel sprig in its mouth, just as Livia had seized the bird. She reared the hen, whose brood named the villa Villa of the Hens, and whose laurel groves supplied Caesars' crowns ever after.

Sergius Sulpicius Galba, who follows, judges with homely wit. He settles a disputed beast of burden by leading it, head muffled, to its watering pond, giving it to the claimant it follows of its own accord after drinking. His war and peace achievements fill the life, but the laurel's end shadows him. Suetonius writes Galba as an old soldier emperor, just, frugal, and doomed by the very signs that announced his rise.
6732-a-lady-s-life-on-a-farm-in-manitoba:
Mrs. Cecil Hall writes home in letters never meant for print, telling an everyday life on a Manitoba farm. Her preface says the letters keep their first shape, not as a literary work, but in hopes their trials may aid future colonists bound for Manitoba or Colorado. A first note, from Queenstown in April, speaks of four hours in harbor to recruit weary forms.

Farm work, weather, neighbors, and the long road from England fill the letters that follow. Hall writes with frank, practical warmth, as a wife and mother learning a new land. A Lady's Life on a Farm in Manitoba is a vivid, first-hand settler's record, useful and touching today.
7099-a-trip-to-manitoba:
Mary Fitzgibbon trips to Manitoba in a book dedicated to Lady Dufferin and introduced with a note on the Canada Pacific Railway. That line, almost an accomplished fact, will cross a thousand miles of prairie in the Swan River and Saskatchewan territories. It will thread the Rockies and run through British Columbia to Vancouver Island, joining Pacific to Atlantic. Land grants beside the line, sold or given to settlers, feed the railway and create populations along its route.

Gladstone's words at West Calder call Manitoba the great province now forming part of the Canadian Dominion. Fitzgibbon writes as a traveler on a new road into a new land, noting cars that carry distant produce to market. The book is a Victorian travel sketch of prairie, railway, and settlement.
a-lady-s-life-on-a-farm-in-manitoba:
Mrs. Cecil Hall explains in her preface that these letters were never intended for publication. They were family letters. She kept them in their original shape. She hoped the experience might help future colonists bound for Manitoba or Colorado. The first is dated at Queenstown on April 14th, written in a four-hour harbour stop on the voyage out, after a cheerless journey to Liverpool in the rain.

From the crossing she writes the whole settler year: the farm, the house, hired help, cooking, visitors, mosquitoes, and the long prairie winter. Hall writes as a lady keeping house where ladies were scarce, honest about loneliness and dirt. Her letters are a woman's firsthand record of Manitoba farming in its pioneer years.
a-trip-to-manitoba:
Mary FitzGibbon travelled from Ontario to the new province of Manitoba and wrote A Trip to Manitoba as a bright, observant travel record, dedicated to Lady Dufferin. Her route runs by rail and steamer through the Great Lakes, then across the prairies and down the Red River to Winnipeg. In the years when the Canadian Pacific Railway was still being built.

Along the way she describes Sault Ste. Marie, Lake Superior in ice, card-sharpers on the cars, and the mud and bustle of early Winnipeg. Later chapters linger on summer and winter life in the town, Icelandic emigrants, giant vegetables, balls at forty below, and the first steamer of the season. A prefatory note praises free land grants and the settlers then filling the province.
britannica-1911-aba: Aba is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and the entry gives the one word three distinct senses. First, it names a form of altazimuth instrument, for measuring angles in sky and land survey, invented by Antoine d'Abbadie and called after him. Second, it names a rough homespun cloth made in Bulgaria. Third, it names a long coarse shirt worn by Bedouin Arabs. Three trades meet under four letters in this compact notice.
britannica-1911-angussola-sophonisba:
Van Dyck is said to have learned more of his art's true principles from talking with Sophonisba Angussola than from any other source. Royal favour had come early: in 1560 Philip II called the Italian portrait painter to his Madrid court, where her work won great praise.

Cremona was her birthplace, around 1535, and she died at Palermo in 1626. She painted several fine likenesses of herself; one hangs at Althorp, and other pieces of hers survive at Florence and Madrid. Talent ran through the household, for her three sisters also won fame as artists, making Cremona home to a remarkable family of women painters.
britannica-1911-cheduba:
Cheduba is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an island in the Bay of Bengal, also called Man aung. It lies ten miles off the coast of Arakan and forms part of the Kyaukpyu district. It runs about 20 miles from north to south and 17 miles across. Its area is 220 square miles, and its people numbered 26,899 in 1901. The channel to the mainland serves boats, but not large vessels.

The interior is richly varied by hill and dale, and southern heights pass a thousand feet. Signs of old volcanic action dot the coast, in earthy cones that give out springs of muddy, gas bubbling water. Copper, iron, and silver ore have been found. The island is noted above all for its petroleum wells. The oil is of excellent quality and is used in paint, since it guards wood against insects. Rice is the staple crop and the chief export.
britannica-1911-copaiba:
Copaiba is an oleo-resin, at times called a balsam, drawn from the trunk of Copaifera trees. The chief species is Copaifera Lansdorfii, of the legume order. Other species grow in the West Indies and in the Amazon valley. The stuff is a thick, clear liquid of light yellow to pale gold hue. At times it shows a faint glow of colour.

Its smell is sharp and its own, and its taste is harsh and bitter. It will not dissolve in water. Alcohol, ether and oils take it up with ease. More than half of it is a volatile oil. Less than half is resin. Drug books list set doses for the resin and for its oil. The oil counts as the weaker drug of the two. Bad taste and harsh action on the gut mark its use. Care in timing its dose closes the entry.
britannica-1911-hecuba:
Hecuba was the wife of Priam, king of Troy. Her father was Dymas, a Phrygian king, by one account. Other accounts name Cisseus or the river-god Sangarius. Homer makes her mother of nineteen of Priam's fifty sons. When Troy fell and Priam was slain, the Greeks took her prisoner. Her later fate is told in many conflicting ways. Most versions connect her with Cynossema on the Hellespont.

Euripides gives the darkest version in his Hecuba. Her youngest son Polydorus had been entrusted to Polymestor of Thrace. She discovered that Polymestor had murdered the boy. In revenge she blinded him and killed his two sons. Agamemnon acquitted her of those acts. Polymestor foretold she would become a dog. Other tales give her to Odysseus or have her drown herself. The transformation hints she was once a goddess with sacred dogs.
britannica-1911-kolaba:
Kolaba, also written Colaba, is a district of British India in the southern division of Bombay, with its headquarters at Alibagh. It covers 2131 square miles and held 605,566 people in 1901. The district lies between the Western Ghats and the sea and is full of hills. Its 20 miles of coast are fringed with coco-nut and betel-nut palms. Along the salt-water creeks stretch tracts of salt marsh, some reclaimed and some used for making salt.

Tidal inlets such as the Nagothna, the Roha or Chaul and the Bankot creek run 30 or 40 miles inland. They carry a brisk trade in rice, salt, firewood and dried fish. The Ghats hold two noted peaks, Raigarh, where Sivaji built his capital, and Miradongar. The name comes from a small island off Alibagh, once a stronghold of Angria, the Mahratta pirate of the 18th century.
cappy-ricks-retires-but-that-doesn-t-kee:
Cappy Ricks Retires, by Peter B Kyne, brings back the Blue Star Navigation Company and everyone who ever shouted into its telephones. Kyne opens with Captain Matt Peasley's log entry recording that he alone survived of the ship's company. Then Murphy returns. Murphy was chief kicker, meaning complainer in chief, of the barkentine Retriever. Now he is marked for promotion to steam, as master of the great freighter Narcissus.

Matt Peasley bought that ship at a ridiculously low figure. He rode the purchase into the presidency of the company. Cappy himself, retired in name, keeps finding two million dollar reasons to return. The illustrations promise Cappy finding his girl a rich husband and J Augustus Redell crying out a fortune. Kyne's shipping world runs on such energy: old sail men, new steam money, and a founder whose retirement lasts exactly as long as his patience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abba: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abba explains the Aramaic word for father, which occurs three times in the New Testament: in Mark, Romans and Galatians. In each case the Greek translation follows, giving abba ho pater in Greek, abba pater in the Latin Vulgate, and Abba, Father in English. St. Paul took up the double form from the early Christians, who had taken it from Christ's prayer, though opinions differ on why the double form appears.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ales-and-terr:
The Diocese of Ales and Terralba in Sardinia is made up of 42 communes in the province of Cagliari, under the Archbishopric of Oristano. The two sees were united by Julius II in 1503. Christianity may have reached Sardinia through groups of believers condemned to work in its mines, and Gregory the Great mentions the see of Ales in a letter of 591. After that nothing is known until 1147, when Bishop Rello appears in a diploma.

Local tradition at Terralba remembers Bishop Mariano, who built the cathedral about 1144. The diocese in the entry's day contained 42 parishes, 102 priests, and 59,530 inhabitants. Its sources run from Cappelletti's Churches of Italy to Sardinian church histories of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvaro-alonzo:
Alvaro Alonzo Barba, secular priest of Andalusian origin from Lepe, lived at Potosí when its silver mines were most productive. Luxury and revelry among Spaniards and mine owners then neared their climax. Amid that sensual turmoil he split his time between priestly duties and close study of the region's ores and their treatment. Since 1570 quicksilver had revolutionized silver-ore treatment, with improvements Barba knew well.

In 1640 he published at Madrid his Arte de los Metales, still valuable as the first work on South American ores and minerals, though metallurgic and out of date. Miners and prospectors still profit from many of its indications, especially on Bolivian mineral localities. It was republished in Spanish in 1729 and 1770 and recently in Chile, with French and English translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-tr:
Basque poet and storyteller Antonio de Trueba, born at Montellana in 1821 and dead at Bilbao in 1889, left his home for Madrid in 1836 hoping to live by writing. He worked as a clerk in a small trading house while filling his spare hours with short poems and tales full of longing for his native Biscay. Queen Isabella II, won by the charm of his writing, made him historiographer, or official historian, of the Biscayan district, a post he held until her flight in 1868.

His Book of Songs, published in 1852, fixed his popularity. Collections of tales followed in 1859, 1860, and 1866, at their best when they deal with his home region and its people. Longer novels, including one on the Cid, hero of Spanish legend and history, failed, the article judges, because he recorded the past too faithfully to let fancy roam. He remains an amiable writer of the second rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cochabamba:
Cochabamba, a diocese of Bolivia, takes its name from the city that is capital of the department of Cochabamba. Founded in 1563 and first called Oropesa, the city stands on the Rio de la Rocha and ranks as the republic's second largest city and a leading commercial centre. By the census of 1902 its population passed 40,000, practically all Catholics. Pius the Ninth erected the Diocese of Cochabamba by bull on 25 June 1847, suffragan to Charcas, or La Plata.

It was Bolivia's fourth diocese, after the Archdiocese of Charcas and the Dioceses of La Paz and Santa Cruz, created early in the seventeenth century. The diocese covers the department of Cochabamba and part of adjoining Beni. Its population, mostly Catholic, passed 330,000 in 1902. Besides schools and charitable institutions, the diocese holds 55 parishes, 80 churches and chapels, and 160 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuba:
A country entry calls Cuba the Pearl of the Antilles, the West Indies' largest and westernmost island, about the size of England. Lying at the mouth of the Gulf of Mexico, it stretches nearly 750 miles east to west and is divided into six provinces, from Pinar del Rio to Santiago de Cuba.

Sections cover coastline and harbours, history from Columbus's landing in 1492 through Spanish rule, agriculture led by sugar, tobacco, and fruit, transport, and population, counted at 1,572,797 in 1899. Religion traces the diocese founded in 1518, and education follows Jesuit colleges and seminaries. The entry gives a full portrait of the island on the eve of its republican era.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuyaba:
A diocesan entry describes Cuyaba, a suffragan see of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. The city, founded by miners around 1720, became capital of Matto Grosso province in 1840, with a population just over 18,000. A prelature erected by Benedict XIV in 1745 was raised to a bishopric by Leo XII in 1826.

The diocese embraces the whole province of Matto Grosso, an area of 532,705 square miles, with a Catholic population of 100,700. It counted 17 parishes, 20 churches, and only 22 priests, 12 diocesan and 10 regular, at the time of writing. The entry is brief, giving the bare framework of a vast and thinly served Brazilian see, with standard references for further detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-danaba:
A short entry describes Danaba, a titular see of Phoenicia Secunda. Ptolemy lists it as a town in Palmyra's territory, and Peutinger's table calls it Danova, a Roman military post between Damascus and Palmyra, twenty miles from Nezala. An Antiochene list of bishoprics from the sixth century makes it a suffragan of Damascus, a rank it kept perhaps into the tenth century.

Only two holders are known. Theodore attended Chalcedon in 451 and signed the province's letter to Emperor Leo I in 458. Eulogius attended the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. Today Danaba is probably Hafer, a village five miles south-east of Sadad in the Damascus region, where about 300 Jacobite Syrians live, most of them now Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elba:
Elba is the largest island of the Tuscan Archipelago, now in the Italian province of Leghorn and cut off from the mainland by the channel of Piombino. Treeless mountain ranges cross it, rising to Monte Capanne at about three thousand three hundred and forty-three feet, and its area is eighty-six square miles. The census of 1901 counted twenty-five thousand five hundred and fifty-six people there, mostly Catholics.

Its chief town is Porto Ferrajo on the north coast, with Porto Longone and Rio as the next towns, and the island belongs to the diocese of Massa Marittima, with eleven parishes. Iron ore, famous since ancient times, is its chief wealth, though lack of fuel means it is smelted on the mainland. Wheat, maize, wine, and warm-climate fruits grow there, tunny and anchovy fishing pays well, and five ports handled over two thousand five hundred merchant ships in 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faltonia-prob:
Faltonia Proba was a fourth-century Christian poetess of aristocratic birth. Her very name is doubtful, since the manuscripts call her simply Proba. Born a pagan, she later became a Christian convert. She wrote a lost epic on Constantine's war with Magnentius.

Her surviving work is a Virgilian cento, verses stitched from Virgil's lines. In hexameters it retells Creation, the Fall, the Deluge, and Christ's life. The poem stayed popular through the Middle Ages despite its constrained action. Proba shows how a Roman lady of high rank turned pagan poetry to Christian ends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girba:
Girba is a titular see in the province of African Tripoli, on the island now called Djerba, known in ancient times as Meninx. The island held three principal cities, Meninx, Tipasa, and Girba, from which it takes its present name. At least two of its bishops are known, Monnulus and Vincent, who attended the Councils of Carthage in 255 and 525. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces the island from antiquity to a French protectorate.

In the seventh century it appears as Terepiton, a corrupt form of Gergiton or Gerbiton. Christians of Sicily and Aragon disputed it with the Arabs through the Middle Ages, and Spaniards seized it several times in the sixteenth century. In 1560 the corsair Dragut surprised the Spanish fleet, and the Turks built a pyramid of the slain's bones, the fortress of the skulls. Today the island counts forty thousand souls, several hundred of them Maltese Catholic sponge-fishers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lyrba:
Lyrba, a titular see of Pamphylia Prima, survives in coinage and in the writings of Dionysius, Ptolemy, and Hierocles. Where exactly it stood, and its full story, remain unknown, though Seidi Shehir, a small modern town in the vilayet of Konia, is a likely match.

Through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the Notitiae episcopatuum rank it under Side. Two bishops are known: Caius, at Constantinople in 381, and Taurianus, at Ephesus in 431. Zeuxius, once listed here, belonged to Syedra. South-east of Kiesme, ruins yield inscriptions, tombs, and traces of a Byzantine church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manitoba:
Manitoba was one of Canada's smallest provinces, yet among its most important in wealth and story. Its name comes from two Sauteux words meaning Manitou Narrows, first given to its lake. Though jokingly called the postage-stamp province, it spans 74,000 square miles, only 8,782 less than England and Scotland together.

Level plains and shallow lakes mark its face, above all Winnipeg, Winnipegosis, and Manitoba lakes. Its climate is bracing, with long, severe, but dry winters. By February 1910 it held 466,368 people, including 51,794 Catholics in May 1909. Rival fur companies merged in 1821, a Council of Assiniboia followed in 1833, and Metis anger at Hudson's Bay monopoly flared in 1849. In 1890 the legislature ignored Catholic school rights, despite the constitution, and a compromise after a Privy Council ruling in 1895 fell short of Catholic hopes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obba: Obba, a titular see in Byzacena in North Africa, is the modern Ebba. It lies on the highway from Carthage to Theveste, seven miles from Lares and sixteen from Althiburus. Mentioned by Polybius as Abba and by Livy, it is known for three bishops: Paul at Carthage in 225, the Donatist Felicissimus in 411, and Valerianus at Constantinople in 553.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olba:
Olba, a titular see in Isauria suffragan to Seleucia, was a city of Cilicia whose priests of Zeus once ruled as kings. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Olbasa, Hierocles Olbe, and Basil of Seleucia Olba, while its oldest name, Ourba or Orba, survives in Ourbanopolis.

Made a Roman colony, its ruins north of Selefkeh are now called Oura. Le Quien names four bishops from the fourth to the seventh centuries, and lists of bishoprics mention the see until the thirteenth century. Those ruins, in the vilayet of Adana, still bear the name Oura.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parahyba:
Parahyba is a Brazilian diocese, suffragan of Bahia, founded on 27 July 1892 from the Diocese of Olinda. It matches the State of Parahyba, one of Brazil's smallest, on the Atlantic, bounded by Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco, and Ceara, covering 28,850 square miles. Its chief city, also the state capital, dates from a Portuguese settlement of 1579, spread over a plateau and a plain, with its port of Cabedello forming the business quarter.

Sugar, cacao, rice, and tobacco grow on the coast, while forested slopes rise behind the town. Chief church buildings are the cathedral of Our Lady of the Snows and the old Jesuit college, now state offices. Its first bishop, Miranda Henriques, born in 1855 and trained at Rome's Pio-Latino college, took charge in March 1894. The diocese counted 735,572 Catholics in 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-riobamba:
Riobamba is a diocese in Ecuador, suffragan to Quito, erected by Pius IX on 5 January 1863. Its city stands 9,039 feet above sea level, 85 miles east-northeast of Guayaquil, with wide streets and low adobe houses built to withstand frequent earthquakes. The old city, eighteen miles west near Cajabamba, once held 40,000 people but was utterly destroyed by an earthquake on 4 February 1797.

Old Riobamba had been capital of the Puruha kingdom before the Incas, and it was burned by Ruminiahui in retreat in 1533. The new city's cathedral and Redemptorist church are praised as very beautiful. The historian Velasco and the poets Larrea and Orozco were natives, and the first national Ecuadorian convention met here in 1830. The diocese covers the provinces of Chimborazo and Bolivar, with 63 priests, 48 churches and chapels, and about 200,000 inhabitants. Its bishop at the time of writing was Andres Machado, appointed in 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-columba:
St. Columba was abbot of Iona, born at Garten, County Donegal, Ireland, on 7 December 521. He died 9 June 597. This entry follows a man of the Clan O'Donnell and of royal descent. His father was Fedhlimdh and his mother Eithne. On his father's side he descended from Niall of the Nine Hostages, a fourth-century Irish king, as his great-great-grandson.

His baptismal name, Colum, means a dove, giving the latinized Columba; Colum-cille is another form, its suffix meaning of the Churches. Cruithnechan, a priest who later became his tutor or foster-father, baptized him at Tulach-Dubhglaise, now Temple-Douglas. Once far enough along in letters, he entered Movilla's monastic school under St. Finnian, who had studied at St. Ninian's Magnum Monasterium on Galloway's shores.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uberaba:
Uberaba is a Brazilian diocese in the state of Minas Gerais, created by a decree of 29 September 1907. It was formed from the diocese of Goiaz, with parishes added from Diamantina. It took in the region known as the Triangulo Mineiro, a wedge of land between great rivers and mountain ranges. The entry maps its bounds river by river and range by range, and counts its Catholic population at 200,000 souls in 1911.

Its first bishop was Eduardo Duarte Silva, born at Florianopolis in 1852. He trained at the Pio-Latino College in Rome and was ordained priest in 1878. The account follows his career to Uberaba and lists the diocese's parishes, clergy, and religious houses. Short and factual, it serves readers tracing the growth of the church in Brazil's interior, where new sees were cut from older ones to match a spreading population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urubamba:
Urubamba, under its full title the Missions of Santo Domingo de Urubamba and Madre de Dios, was a prefecture apostolic created by the Holy See in 1899 at Peru's request. On 10 April 1902 three Dominican fathers from the Spanish province took charge of the missions. Their number gradually grew to eleven, ten Spaniards and one Peruvian, with more recruits expected. The vast territory and the peoples to be civilized and evangelized demanded still more hands.

All the missionaries answered to the prefect apostolic, Father Ramon Zubieta. His efforts did much for progress in civilization and for the religious and geographical survey of the Montana region in eastern Peru. The entry lists the stations and the work in hand, giving a snapshot of a young Dominican mission on Peru's forest frontier.
colomba:
Prosper Mérimée set his novella Colomba in Corsica, the island of the vendetta, and translated here by Lady Mary Loyd. Colonel Sir Thomas Nevil and his daughter Lydia land at Marseilles fresh from Italy, which Lydia finds lacking in local color. In Corsica they meet Orso della Rebbia, a young officer home on leave, and his sister Colomba, who nurses the family's blood feud for their murdered father.

Colomba presses her brother toward vengeance while Lydia draws him toward law and love. Mérimée stages the contest between Corsican honor and modern manners with dry, exact irony. The epigraph, a Corsican death-song, sets the terms: peace requires someone to forgo revenge. Colomba herself, proud, poetic, and relentless, dominates every scene she enters.

modern-skepticism-a-journey-through-the-:
Joseph Barker published this spiritual autobiography at Philadelphia in 1874. Its subtitle tells the arc: a trip through the land of doubt and back again. The first chapter tells his early life: entering the church, the ministry, and happy days. Then came a sad change, and Barker asks how it happened.

His second chapter catalogs the causes of unbelief. He names vice, inborn tendencies to doubt, and disappointed hopes. He also blames creeds that misrepresent Christ, church divisions, and ignorant defenders of the faith. False science completes his list. Barker, once a noted preacher turned skeptic, writes his return to faith as a cautionary life story.
mythology-of-aryan-nations-chowkhamba:
The Reverend George Cox wrote The Mythology of the Aryan Nations in the Victorian age. The Chowkhamba house in India later reprinted his survey. Cox was a clergyman drawn to the science of myth.

He compares tales from India, Persia, Greece, and the North. Sun heroes and dawn maidens recur in his scheme. Like many of his day, he read most myths as weather stories. That theory is dated now, yet the gathered tales retain value. The book shows comparative myth at its boldest, and why later scholars had to rebuild the field.
nasa-tm-19670003832-propellant-feed-duct:
P. L. Muller Jr., of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, describes the plumbing of the Saturn rockets in this memorandum. His subject is the ducting that carries liquid propellant from the tanks to the engines. He also covers the flexible lines that let the engines swivel, or gimbal, to steer the vehicle.

Muller describes the feed system concepts and layouts used on the Saturn V. For the gimbal lines, he traces the line of designs from the Jupiter vehicle through the Saturn I. The Saturn V systems are the most sophisticated in that line. He notes that future vehicles' feed systems will build on Saturn V work.

the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Sergius Sulpicius Galba opens the seventh volume of Suetonius's Lives, in the Thomson translation revised by T. Forester. Suetonius begins by declaring Nero the last of the Caesars' line, an end he says was foretold by signs. An eagle once dropped a hen holding a sprig of laurel into Livia's lap at her villa at Veii. The hen reared so many chickens that the place was still called the Villa of the Hens.

Laurels from that grove supplied the Caesars' triumphal crowns, and each emperor planted a new tree after a triumph. In Nero's last year the whole plantation withered to the roots and the hens died. Suetonius uses omens to mark the end of one dynasty and the brief opening of Galba's.

un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Background opens the privacy part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. It sets the scene in a few strokes. For solid goods, law guards the owner's stake. For facts, law must also weigh the people the facts describe.

Before computers, that second stake won scant cover. Libel law was nearly the whole shield. From the 1970s on, machines made it cheap to gather, store, match, and send vast files on a person. Fresh threats to privacy came with that power. States replied with office rules, civil suits, and some new crimes. World bodies then pushed for a shared line, as the next parts show.
